8 is the clotting factor not working in patients with haemophilia A. Haemophilia is a disease of the blood clotting system. It mainly affects males but can occur in females as well. It causes uncontrolled bleeding due to a deficiency or dysfunction of a clotting factor. There are different types of haemophilia depending on which clotting factor isn't working properly - there are A, B, C (and D but this is very rare) types of haemophilia. For example, haemophilia A is caused by reduced/no clotting factor 8. Clotting factors work in a cascade to form a soft clot, then a fibrin clot. So factor 8 works in the intrinsic pathway to activate factor X. If you have a deficiency of factor 8 you won't be able to form a clot so will experience uncontrolled bleeding.  Haemophilic people often have a low level of factor VIII in their plasma and have high levels of von Willebrand factor in their blood. Von Willebrand factor is essential for adhesion of platelets to the endothelium of damaged vessels. This means that even though the factor VIII levels are low, the von Willebrand factor levels help maintain haemostasis to some extent.  Treatment of Haemophilia A involves infusions of factor 8 concentrates. If left untreated it can lead to arthritis, joint deformity and damage to other tissues and organs. It is also slower to respond to a second infection because the time is needed to identify the specific antigen. However, once mounted, it is more effective at clearing the pathogen. Spina bifida is caused by failure of neural tube fusion during the fourth and fifth weeks of gestation. It may be associated with other abnormalities, including anencephaly (absence of the major part of the skull), meningocele (protrusion of the spinal cord through the vertebral column without opening of the overlying membranes), and myelomeningocele (the most common form of spina bifida, in which there is exposure of the laminae and the dura mater). Occasionally, it may occur after birth as a result of mechanical trauma or infection. Spina bifida occulta occurs when only a small portion of the vertebra does not fuse properly around the spinal nerves. In this case, the spinal nerves are covered by bone and skin, but a small gap (spina bifida) is present. This is usually asymptomatic, but occasionally can cause pain and tingling in the lower extremities. A small number of patients develop incontinence of urine because of the proximity of the bladder to the exposed nerve roots. It is stimulated by the presence of phospholamban and therefore phospholamban is involved in the 'uphill' transport of Ca2+ into the SR. This uphill transport is important because it means that the heart does not waste energy pumping out large amounts of Ca2+ into the cytoplasm (which would happen if there was no uphill transport). The uphill transport means that only a small amount of Ca2+ is required to be pumped out of the cytosol and into the SR. This is important because Ca2+ is very energetically expensive to move around the body. If we didn't have uphill transport, then all the energy used up by pumping Ca2+ out of the cytoplasm would not allow us to do much work! So instead of using lots of ATP on pumping Ca2+ out of cells, we use less ATP on pumping it into them. This means that while other tissues use up lots of energy moving things around their bodies (like blood), our hearts don't need too much extra energy doing this job - they just need enough energy so that when they contract they don't get tired too quickly! Foramen ovale closes due to the increased pressure in the left atrium which forces blood into the right atrium via the foramen ovale. Pericarditis is inflammation of the pericardium. It may be idiopathic or due to infection (viral/bacterial), metastatic cancer, trauma, autoimmune disorders, neoplasm, constrictive pericarditis, pericarditis after myocardial infarction (MI) or after cardiac surgery. The classic presentation is chest pain, typically worse on inspiration and lying down, shortness of breath and swelling of the feet. Other symptoms include fever, nausea and vomiting and a dry cough. On examination there may be pulsus paradoxus (reduced chest movement during respiration). Cardiac markers are usually normal. It is important to distinguish between acute and chronic forms of pericarditis. Acute pericarditis is associated with effusion (fluid build up within the pericardial space) of any amount. Effusions <150ml are called small effusions and those >150ml are called large effusions. If the fluid accumulates rapidly it can cause tamponade (compression of the heart muscle). This results in reduced output and blood pressure falls. Treatment is with diuretics, colchicine and corticosteroids. In severe cases pericardiocentesis (removal of the fluid from the pericardial cavity) may be necessary. Chronic pericarditis is characterised by inflammation of the pericardium without effusion. It is often asymptomatic but may present with chest pain (typically exertional), palpitations and dyspnoea. Echocardiography shows changes including thickening of the pericardium, pericardial effusion, impaired ventricular filling and diastolic dysfunction. Treatment is with colchicine and corticosteroids. Pericarditis can lead to conduction disturbances, myocardial infarction and arrhythmias. Pericarditis after MI is associated with increased risk of mortality. Complications include cardiac tamponade, constrictive pericarditis and chronic pericarditis. Pericarditis should be differentiated from other causes of retrosternal chest
